record.title: MiRL targets recurring terminal-agent errors during reinforcement learning
record.summary: A new preprint proposes Misbehavior-driven RL (MiRL), which profiles recurring errors in a terminal agent, resumes training rollouts from replayable prefixes before those errors, and requires both task-test success and avoidance of the target behavior for reward. On Qwen3.5-4B, the authors report 51.8% on Terminal-Bench Lite and 21.3% on Terminal-Bench 2.1 using 35% of TMax-4B's rollouts; a separate 16-seed result strengthens only the Terminal-Bench 2.1 comparison. Results are from one model backbone and no independent reproduction was performed.
organizations: University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill

claims.label: DEMONSTRATED
claims.text: The authors posted arXiv:2610.35697v1 on 2026-10-26 and describe Misbehavior-driven RL (MiRL), which profiles recurring terminal-agent errors, starts training rollouts from replayable prefixes immediately before those errors, and rewards a rollout only when it passes task tests and a behavior judge says it avoided the target misbehavior.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: On Qwen3.5-4B, the authors report that eight recurring error types cover 52.1% of profiled wrong steps. With 189 retained training environments, MiRL scores 51.8% on Terminal-Bench Lite and 21.3% on Terminal-Bench 2.1, versus their TMax-4B results of 47.4% and 20.6%, using 35% of TMax-4B's rollouts. A separate 16-seed Terminal-Bench 2.1 comparison reports means of 21.14% for MiRL and 20.22% for TMax-4B.

claims.label: NOT_ESTABLISHED
claims.text: The preprint does not establish that the gains transfer to other model backbones or agent domains, remain stable across independent training runs, or persist when prefix-retention bias and checkpoint selection are controlled. Its reported benchmark results are not independent confirmation.

evidence_gaps.description: No independent reproduction of MiRL or its reported benchmark results was inspected.
Each training recipe was trained once; the 3-run headline error bars cover evaluation runs, not variation across separately trained policies. The 16-seed evaluation covers TB-2.1 only.
Only Qwen3.5-4B was tested, and exact-output prefix replay retains 219 of 640 candidate prefixes, which may bias training toward deterministic environments.

brief.importance_rationale: If the reported gains transfer beyond one 4B terminal-agent backbone, using recurring policy errors to target rollout states and behavioral rewards could change how post-training data and compute are allocated. The reported advantage is material on Terminal-Bench Lite, while cross-backbone transfer and training-run variance remain unestablished.
limitations: Author-reported preprint results; no independent reproduction was performed in this activation.
Only one policy backbone, Qwen3.5-4B, was tested.
Training recipes were each run once; the standard three evaluation runs do not measure training-seed variance.
Only 219 of 640 candidate prefixes passed exact-output replay, potentially biasing retained examples toward deterministic environments.
Headline checkpoint selection uses Terminal-Bench Lite score among the top five smoothed-reward checkpoints, so TB-Lite is involved in model selection.
The 16-seed evaluation addresses Terminal-Bench 2.1 only; its small mean gap does not establish a broad advantage.
organizations: University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill
brief.summary: A new preprint proposes Misbehavior-driven RL (MiRL), which profiles recurring errors in a terminal agent, resumes training rollouts from replayable prefixes before those errors, and requires both task-test success and avoidance of the target behavior for reward. On Qwen3.5-4B, the authors report 51.8% on Terminal-Bench Lite and 21.3% on Terminal-Bench 2.1 using 35% of TMax-4B's rollouts; a separate 16-seed result strengthens only the Terminal-Bench 2.1 comparison. Results are from one model backbone and no independent reproduction was performed.

technical.claimed_result: For Qwen3.5-4B terminal-agent training, the authors report that MiRL reduces measured recurring misbehaviors by 43–57% on average on unseen prefixes, exceeds TMax-4B by 4.4 percentage points on Terminal-Bench Lite, and is close on Terminal-Bench 2.1 (21.3% versus 20.6%). Their additional 16-seed TB-2.1 evaluation reports 21.14% versus 20.22%.
technical.compute_or_cost: The paper reports 35% as many rollouts and 39% of TMax-4B's GPU hours. MiRL's author-calculated total cost is $1,960; this is 56% of TMax-4B's reported relative cost. The paper states that TMax-4B totals are estimated from the prior paper's settings and curves and its own measured throughput, while policy tokens are priced as a service and GPU hours are reported separately. MiRL cost more than PivotRL ($999) and RaR+ ($770). No independent cost recomputation was performed.
technical.demonstrated_result: The arXiv preprint and a public Apache-2.0 code repository and model checkpoint are available. The performance and error-reduction measurements are reported by the authors and were not reproduced here. The authors’ README and checkpoint card document setup and serving; the released checkpoint is language-model-only. Neither code nor weights were run in this activation.
technical.mechanism: MiRL first groups profiled policy errors into recurring misbehavior types. It then starts on-policy rollouts from prefixes before a target misbehavior, retaining prefixes only when commands replay with exact recorded outputs, and gives reward only when task tests pass and a behavior judge confirms the target behavior was avoided.
technical.regime: Qwen3.5-4B on long-horizon terminal tasks in shell-container environments. Error profiling uses 2,017 environments; 640 candidate prefixes were tested for replay and 219 from 189 environments were retained. Benchmarks are Terminal-Bench Lite (100 tasks) and Terminal-Bench 2.1 (89 tasks). Standard headline comparisons average three evaluation runs; an additional 16-seed comparison is reported only for TB-2.1. The authors’ README reports an 8× A100 80 GB setup, 96 CPU threads, about 1 TB RAM and 5 TB local disk; it identifies Qwen3.5-4B as policy and Qwen3.8-27B as error localizer/teacher, and fixes the TMax code revision at 7387d2f9142397a458dc39f0827a2ab0b4c03cda. The README identifies API-key requirements; the behavior judge is Gemini 3.8 Flash. These are author-documented setup facts, not independently checked runtime requirements.
technical.strongest_baseline: TMax-4B is the principal scaled-data baseline. On the authors' evaluation hardware it scores 47.4% on TB-Lite and 20.6% on TB-2.1. MiRL is 51.8% and 21.3%, respectively, with 35% of TMax-4B's rollouts. The 16-seed TB-2.1 means are 21.14% and 20.22%; this indicates a small margin on that benchmark, not a decisive broad win.

brief.title: MiRL targets recurring terminal-agent errors during reinforcement learning
brief.why_it_matters: The paper treats failure analysis as a way to allocate training rollouts and reward signals, rather than only as a diagnostic tool. If its result transfers, teams may gain more from selecting where rollouts begin and what they penalize than from scaling environment count alone. The evidence currently supports a bounded result for one terminal-agent backbone, not a general recipe across models or tool domains.
